doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: The Mini Moog and DX-7 democratizing synthesizers
summary: Levin recalls cheap portable synthesizers, the Yamaha DX-7 prototype in Japan, and how arrangers began playing the parts themselves.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: But my feeling at the time was that it changed the industry. It changed the music industry. I played a prototype in Japan, right around then, in 1979, ’80, and it was, I’d been using synthesizers a lot at that point. Analog synthesizers. And they just completely re-thought how this should be done with computer controlled frequency modulation processes, storing sounds in memory. Nobody had ever done that before. And the buttons that you push with multiple menu levels below. We take that all for granted now. I just looked at this thing, they let me use it for a concert, and they said we’ll hook it up, here’s your volume controller. And I’m looking at it, and I just turned to the guy and said, “I don’t know how to work it.”

Yeah there were no knobs, just buttons. And so the guy gave me a demonstration and I caught on to some of it, creating sounds. I did it eventually but I couldn’t do it at the time so I’d call them up. It didn’t sound like anything else. It didn’t perform like anything else. It was great. And when it eventually got here it had this system, you could store sounds on a cartridge and pass them around, share them, steal them. That was the beginning. I got a couple of DX-7s early on in the 80s. And I got a lot of session calls so they paid for themselves quickly. After a year or so I started to realize that I wasn’t getting some of those calls. A lot of the arrangers and producers that were calling me, “Bring your DX- 7,” the studios started to get them so I would just bring a cartridge of sounds and plug my own sounds into it. Then I started to realize I wasn’t getting some of these calls because the arrangers that used to hire me had their own DX-7 and they would just bring it to the studio and play the part themselves. So it’s really been going on I think for twenty years or so, or maybe a little less. And it occurred to me then that maybe this ride wouldn’t go forever. But this is kind of what it’s come to. The technology has changed what we do.
